content.title: Learn How To Become a Postal Inspector in 10 Steps
content.text: Finding a jobLearn How To Become a Postal Inspector in 10 StepsUpdated December 10, 2025What does a postal inspector do?How to become a postal inspector in 10 stepsPostal inspector salaryThe United States Postal Inspection Service is a government agency charged with securing the U.S. Postal Service and its employees. The members of the service, called postal inspectors, are essential for ensuring that U.S. mail arrives intact and that crimes don't occur in relation to the postal service. If you're interested in joining this important agency, it's vital to understand what the job and the application process entail.In this article, we discuss how to become a postal inspector in 10 steps and review the average salary for postal inspectors.What does a postal inspector do?A postal inspector is a member of the United States Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), the law enforcement segment of the U.S. Postal Service. The principal mission of the USPIS is to enforce the criminal statutes that relate to the postal service, postal service employees and its customers. The service is broad and includes the following tasks:Protecting the U.S. Postal Service: A police force within the USPIS secures high-value postal service properties. They also investigate and strive to prevent violence against postal service employees.Preventing illicit narcotic transfer: The USPIS works to prevent the transfer of illicit substances through the mail. The service shares information with other government agencies to improve prevention efforts.Deterring mail, package and identity theft: The postal service aims to deliver all mail and packages in an unopened, intact state, and USPIS investigates and instances of opened, damaged mail. The service also collaborates with other agencies to prevent identity theft, investigate instances of it and prosecute perpetrators.Identifying mail fraud and fraud prevention: Mail fraud refers to efforts to obtain money or valuables fraudulently through the mail. Besides investigating and prosecuting fraud cases, the service tries to prevent cases by educating the public about fraud schemes.Investigating money laundering: The act of laundering money relates to proceeds gained illegally, such as through the sale of illicit goods, counterfeiting, mail fraud, tax evasion and other crimes. When laundering attempts occur through the U.S. mail, the USPIS investigates.Analyzing suspicious mail: The USPIS investigates mail containing potentially hazardous substances, items or devices qualifies as suspicious mail. They also handle any mailed threat directed at targeted individuals or groups.Responding to disaster: In the event of a natural or human-made disaster, the USPIS and the U.S. Postal Service respond by protecting the mail, postal service facilities and postal service employees.Preventing cybercrime: The USPIS includes a cybercrime unit that helps to identify individuals who use U.S. mail or online postal service tools to commit illicit internet trade or other such activities.Securing global mail: The U.S. Postal Service is part of the Universal Postal Union, an agency of the United Nations for which the USPIS provides training and support.Related: 12 Degrees for Government JobsHow to become a postal inspector in 10 stepsRoles with the USPIS are federal government positions. The process is extensive, comprising an application component and a hiring component. Follow these 10 steps to complete the process:1. Make sure you meet the eligibility requirementsA job as a postal inspector requires knowledge of the postal service, problem-solving skills and immense responsibility. Because of the high stakes of this role, the USPIS has an extensive set of requirements, along with a long process for sourcing candidates. A legitimate candidate for a postal inspector role meets the following requirements:At least 21 years old and less than 37 years old at the time of appointment, except for certain veteransPossess a four-year degree from an accredited academic instituteNo record of felonies or domestic violence.In good physical conditionCan write and speak in EnglishHave a valid driver's license, a minimum of two years of unsupervised driving experience and a record of safe drivingWilling to relocateRelated: FAQ: What Are Federal Jobs?2. Check for openings and applyWhen there are openings for postal inspectors, a notification shows at the top of the USPIS website home page. If no openings are available, the page reads that the application's closed. In that case, try to check the site regularly to watch for any openings. You may also subscribe to the USPIS mailing list to receive employment announcements and alerts. When a position becomes available, click on the link and follow the steps to create your profile and complete the application.Related: How To Fill Out an Online Job Application3. Complete the first part of the entrance examIf the USPIS accepts your application, you receive a notification via an email containing a link to an entrance examination. This is the first of a two-part timed, multiple-choice test, which you're to complete within 72 hours of receipt. Follow all the instructions on the screen, and complete the exam within the specified time frame.Related: 18 Post Office Jobs To Consider (Plus Salaries and Duties)4. Complete the eCAPIf you pass the first entrance examination, you receive another email containing another link. This one is for the eCAP—the Electronic Comprehensive Application Packet—a collection of personal documents the USPIS requires candidates to submit. Follow the provided instructions so you don't forget a step. You have five days, or 120 hours, from the point of receipt to complete the eCAP.Related: Postal Inspector Skills: Definition and Tips5. Complete Standard Form 86Standard Form 86 is the official U.S. Questionnaire for National Security, for which the USPIS sends you a link after you submit your eCAP. The purpose of the form is for the federal government to collect information about you. The government uses this information to conduct background investigations and evaluations of your character before determining whether you're eligible to hold a national security position, such as that of a postal inspector. From the point of receipt, you have 168 hours, or seven days, to complete the questionnaire.6. Accept the invitation and attend the Information ExchangeAfter you submit Standard Form 86, a field recruiter from the USPIS typically contacts you via email concerning an event called an Information Exchange. Upon receipt of this invitation, you have 48 hours to accept. If you don't accept the invitation, you can lose your spot in the application process.At the Information Exchange, you take the second and final part of the entrance exam; the business writing test and the language exam. The timed second part is multiple choice. A passing score qualifies you to take the business writing test. Follow any provided instructions to complete both assessments. If you stated on your application that you can speak a foreign language, you can expect to take a language exam as well. This exam confirms your proficiency in the specified language.Related: 8 Examples of Business Writing7. Complete the further evaluationIf you've been successful up to this point, the USPIS invites you to the Assessment Center in Potomac, Maryland, to undergo an in-person evaluation of your knowledge and skills. This involves a physical assessment, polygraph interview and management interview. If you pass this evaluation, you can expect to undergo a polygraph test to confirm the information you provided on Standard Form 86. To close the application process, the USPIS may invite you for an interview with USPIS managers.During the interview, you can expect to answer questions about the role of a postal inspector, the training required for the job and general or behavior-related topics. If you pass this final evaluation, the USPIS places you in its selection pool for two years. This means that the service considers you a potential hire and may consider giving you a job offer.Related: Tips for Success on Employment Polygraph Tests8. Accept the conditional employment offerIf the USPIS hires you, they begin by extending a conditional employment offer, in which case your employment status depends on the successful completion of a drug screening and a medical examination scheduled by the service. These evaluations are to confirm eligibility requirements concerning drug use and physical fitness. Since these exams directly relate to your chances of securing a role, it's best to comply with all the instructions given by the USPIS.Related: What To Expect from a Pre-Employment Screening9. Pass the background investigationDuring this stage, the USPIS also conducts top secret clearance, a background investigation comprising investigations into your background. The clearance portion requires no additional activity on your part. It's common for the USPIS to contact you after the background check. Checks evaluated during the background investigation include:Credit checksCriminal historyPersonal interviews with associatesPersonal and business reference checksPast employer checksNeighbor checksVerification of educationRelated: How Long Do Pre-Employment Background Checks Take?10. Complete Basic Instructor TrainingUpon successful completion of all the previous steps, you receive an appointment letter and invitation to the 16-week Basic Instructor Training program in Potomac. This is a residential program that covers topics such as firearms, defensive tactics, academics, physical fitness and practical exercises. Once you graduate from the program, the USPIS assigns you your duty location, where you report and begin your career as a U.S. postal inspector.Postal inspector salaryThe average salary for a postal inspector is $135,544 per year. It's important to note that your location, experience and qualifications may impact this salary. Government employees also receive generous federal benefits, including paid time off, health insurance and a retirement pension.For the most up-to-date salary information from Indeed, click on the link provided.The information on this site is provided as a courtesy and for informational purposes only.
